And to show that these are not words of insult, but of truth and rebuke, listen to Paul, the great preacher, who says: “Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers.”

May believers be enlightened, and opponents be humbled and turn back. There is no need for toil: humble yourself before the word and receive salvation. God once threatened the people of Jerusalem through the prophet, saying, “Behold, I shall destroy them and reduce them to nothing.” And when the Lord saw that their hearts had repented, the Lord said to the man of God, “Do you see how they have humbled themselves? I too shall not destroy them.” Through the prayers of the holy fathers, may they turn back, may we be strengthened, and may the Church be glorified in Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

Let us see where the Jews stand and what condition the Christians are in. Listen to the holy Gospel: “Whoever believes in the Son,” it says, “receives eternal life; and whoever disobeys the Son does not see life.” The living celebrate a feast with the dead. What good have the Jews devised? What order of worship have they preserved uncorrupted, so that you might draw from them beautiful practices to add as a necessary support to the Church? Do you not hear the prophet saying, “You, house of Israel, have acted perversely throughout your youth and falsified the truth”? For they denied the worship of God and sold it, because they paid no heed. Indeed, they did not even keep their wine pure. Is this not the very first accusation against them in the prophet Isaiah? “Your merchants,” he says, “mix water with wine.” If only the heretics now mixed water with wine, and not God with created beings! See the prophets’ written accusation against the Jews, which the apostles also proclaim openly. Listen to the great preacher Paul, who writes to the Thessalonians: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that you too have suffered the same things from your own people as the Church of God has from the Jews—from the Jews who killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets and persecuted us, who also displeased God and opposed mankind.” Do you become a partner of those who are subject to immeasurable punishments? To such people Isaiah says, “That is your portion, and that is the lot of your inheritance.”

I would like to learn from them why they celebrate the feast at all, and for the sake of what hope, since they do away with repentance. What worship do they practice—vain and [?], the worship of the foolish? They do it without hope of repentance, though they need repentance more than anyone. Burning with sores, they deny the physician. They go about bearing the name of Cathars, which means “the holy ones,” yet they have holiness neither in body nor in mind. Nothing so provokes God, brings him to anger, and makes someone liable to severe torments as calling oneself holy. Even if someone is free from every sin, he ought to count himself among sinners. Listen to Saint John: “Children, if we sin, we are not of God”; and again, “Whoever does evil is not of God.” After giving instruction not to sin, he then brings forward the truth. The one who said, “Whoever sins is not of God,” lowers himself still further and says this also: “If we say that we have not sinned, we lie.” He gave instruction in watchfulness, and did not deny the power. He looked to the teaching of truth, and also saw how readily the mind stumbles. But now the enemies of honoring God celebrate feasts and demand confirmation for their deeds, while they have strayed from every firm foundation.

I too wished to raise such matters with you who love Christ, and to show that this opposition is futile, an empty opinion. When someone departs from the order of the Church, he does not stand still; rather, error carries him away, like the currents of rivers flowing into the sea. What do Easter and the feast make known? What is accomplished on the day of the feast? Are not Christ’s sufferings and resurrection [?] proclaimed? Salvation is announced to the world, and every soul is enlightened by the divine word. How, then, do we possess this seal and pledge of worship of God on only one day of the year? Is there not an Easter of the Church every Sunday? Surely the sacrifice on that day is not one thing and the sacrifice on this day another? Surely the splendor of the mysteries at Easter is not different from that on Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday? Whenever you commemorate Christ’s sufferings, you celebrate Easter. Formerly, lambs were sacrificed once a year, but Christ’s sacrifice is offered continually. Therefore the giver of life, making it clear that the mystery is not subject to times and days, or months and years, says to the disciples: ‘Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, proclaim my death.’ Who, then, celebrates that feast? Whoever performs this same mystery celebrates Easter continually.

And if they say that the mystery is performed continually, what need is there for a new feast? There is great need. Many times such a thing was given [?] to comfort our human nature and weakness. God’s mystery always remains unchanging and firm, as do the altar, the priests, the sacrifices, the acts of worship, and everything performed in his name. But because God saw human weakness, entangled with earthly matters and defiled by various kinds of impurity, he established a remedy for it through the holy apostles: the feast of Easter. Thus, whoever is always clothed in sins and fastened to earthly cares, and is unwilling to look toward the light of worship of God, might at least take notice through the name of the feast and, by remembering the life-giving sufferings, prepare himself to partake of the holy things.

Feasts exist so that many people may gather in one place, but for the saints there are feasts every day. What is the saints’ feast? To bless God. Therefore, whoever blesses him continually celebrates [?] feasts. And listen to David, who says, “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth.” Whoever blesses [?] always celebrates a feast. The names of Easter, of [?], and of feasts at which everyone assembles indicate the gathering of many in one place: to enlighten those in darkness, to bring back those who have gone astray, to straighten crooked paths, to raise the dead and buried, and, in every way, to build up all the members of Christ. But it is no wonder that those who have broken away from the Church should also separate themselves from the feast. For if they had been of us, they would have remained with us. But the corrupter of the feast will be exposed by the faithful, and our feast will shine brightly at its proper time—not as though grace were subject to particular times, for every order and arrangement is to be established in the Church. Let us now proceed with the discourse. Let us speak and preach, not regarding the preaching as something belonging to ourselves, but rendering service to the holy father. Let us discharge the overdue debt of our father’s discourse. I say this so that no one, being unaware of these circumstances, should blame us for appropriating the times allotted to our father’s teaching. For we do what we are commanded and necessarily follow our father’s wishes.

“MY SHEEP,” says the giver of life, “hear my voice and follow me, and I give them eternal life.” What else can one expect from life but life? What other hope can one receive from light but the rays of light? Or what else can one expect from the fountain of blessings but the goodness of its gifts? Therefore David also says, “With you is the fountain of life, and by the light of your face we see light.” That light is pure and spreads by its nature, sending out many and varied rays of goodness. For it heals the various afflictions of souls and cures the various pains of bodies, because he is the creator of bodies and souls. Just as he granted them a single creation, so he also bestows a single healing. And we can learn from today’s reading how the fountain of good things possesses goodness in himself.

Heretics are an unwatered garden, and however many plants they plant, they are not reliable. Whoever follows not the voice of God but his own thoughts, even if he plants a plant, it is a plant of unbelief. Isaiah bears witness that anyone who does not have the word of God, even if he plants something, is not reliable and faithful. Just as there is a plant of faith, so there is also a plant of unbelief. All the plants of heretics are plants of unbelief, for their thoughts give birth to them. And every right glorification according to the Gospel and the apostles is a plant of faith and reliable seed. Therefore the Giver of Life also said concerning the Jews, “Leave them alone. Every plant that has not been planted by my Father shall be uprooted.” And how did the heavenly Father plant? Through prophets and apostles. And how did Satan plant? Through heretics and the ungodly. Let the plant of ungodliness be uprooted, and let no room be found in Satan’s place. Everything that opposes Christ’s power and rises against it is torn down. Darkness that contends against the light is driven away by the light. But let us come to what lies before us.

The Giver of Life rebuked the cities: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” Let the Gospel say now as well: “Woe to you, Arius! Woe to you, Macedonius! Woe to you, Eunomius! For if the preaching proclaimed among you had been proclaimed in Sodom, perhaps they would have marveled at the Savior, glorified the Benefactor, and recognized the Creator.” Indeed, brothers, we ought not to be angry with the schismatics, but to mourn over them. Listen to the Scripture that says: “Mourn for the dead for seven days, but for the fool and the ungodly all their days.” And who is the fool, the one without understanding? Let David tell us: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” It is not only the pagan who says, “There is no God,” but these people also. For outwardly they say that there is a God, but in practice they do not say that God exists. When a heretic says that Christ is God, but does not consider him God by nature, he says it only in words and has denied it in practice. For they say that Christ is God, but not by nature as the Father is, since the nature of the one is different from the nature of the other. When someone denies in his heart and mind the honor of the Son’s divinity, even though he calls him God, he does not consider him God, for he effaces the true image of divinity with destructive [?].

And now, what should be said about this? Prophecy was spring, as I said before, and the Gospel was the harvest. But do not let the words I spoke yesterday seem strange to you: that the time of the prophets was the time of spring and sowing, and that of the Gospel was the time of summer and harvest. For there are other harvests as well. The prophets sowed, and the apostles reaped after Christ’s coming. Again, God sows, and the angels reap. The apostles became the reapers of the prophets’ sowing, and the angels become the reapers of the Giver of Life’s preaching. The prophets sowed knowledge of things to come; they also sowed the coming of Christ, announcing it beforehand. Christ’s apostles reaped. Christ sowed beforehand the hope of the resurrection. The prophets also sowed the future coming of the Giver of Life. And Christ sowed the future resurrection of the dead and his own second coming. That the apostles became the reapers of the first sowing, and that the angels become the reapers of the second, is stated in his own words: “Behold, the sower went out to sow good seed. Weeds also sprang up alongside it.” And, to cut it short: “At harvest time I will tell the reapers, ‘Gather the weeds separately, and the wheat separately.’” When the disciples asked what the parable meant, he said: “The field is the world, and the one who sowed is the Son of Man. The good seed is the children of the kingdom, and the weeds are the children of the evil one. The harvest is the end of the world.”

And Zechariah does not show the punishments inflicted by the scythe without reason; the Greek calls it a sickle. He says, “I saw a flying scythe, and I said to the angel who was speaking to me, ‘Lord, what is this?’ And he said, ‘These are the curses that go out over the face of the whole earth and consume the liar and his house and everything that belongs to him.’ Why not a sword, a spear, or an arrow, but a sickle? Because a sickle is kept for the harvest, and the reapers, the angels, are sent out and gather the grain. Then the whole world can be seen harvested at once. And from where will they reap? They will draw them out of the graves. They will not cut them apart, but join together those who have been cut apart. Now bodies have been sown in the fields like seeds, as Paul also says: “So it is with the resurrection of the dead: it is sown in corruption and rises without corruption.” And because they were sown in graves, they will be reaped from graves. He says, “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather his chosen ones from the four winds, from the ends of heaven to the ends of the earth.” You will recognize these words in David: “Gather his holy ones to him.” They will gather everyone and bring them together in one place.

Everyone will rise, but some will be placed before the dreadful judgment seat as those condemned to punishment, while others will be caught up to meet the Lord as holy ones. Just as, when a king enters, a condemned person does not dare to appear before the king, while the dignitaries and those held in honor go out to meet him, so also, when the Son of God comes from heaven and appears, the holy ones are caught up into the heights. Thus it will seem that they are coming with him. Just as those who go out to meet a king and return with him seem to have been with him all along, so also, when the holy ones are caught up to meet the Giver of Life, it will seem that they are descending from heaven with him. And who bears witness to this? Paul: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet of God. And the dead will rise first; then we who are alive will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.” See: they go out to meet him and come with him.

And pay attention to these wonders. In this world, those who go out to meet kings go in their own chariots and on their own horses. But the Giver of Life himself sends heavenly envoys—not chariots and horses, but chariots of cloud, his very own. And why do you marvel that Elijah was taken up in fiery chariots, while the apostles and others, one by one, are taken up in chariots of cloud? Do not consider the fiery chariot more honorable than the chariot of cloud. At that time, envoys were sent to the prophet: fiery chariots and fiery horses. He ascended from these heavenly beings into heaven, and like a wheel he rolled upward from below into the heights. But at that time fiery chariots were indeed fitting, whereas afterward they are not fiery but made of cloud. Why? Because at that time the heavenly vessel still had some earthly needs, so that through the fiery chariots it might be renewed, cast off its earthly weight, and receive the lightness of angels; for from then on he was to dwell with the angels themselves. There the envoy was fiery, and here the envoy is made of cloud. For bodies rise without corruption, and therefore they ascend lightly into the cloud. And so that no one may think that we disparage the former and honor the latter, I said that the prophet was honored with fiery chariots, while those who are caught up to meet Christ ascend on clouds. For clouds are the chariots of the holy God. And hear David: he says, “He established his upper chambers upon the waters and made the clouds his means of travel.” He honors the saints with his own chariots. Hear Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud and will come into Egypt.” See that he commands the saints to be honored with his own chariots and to go out to meet the Giver of Life.

And how will they go up? He himself makes it clear, for Paul never speaks on his own authority, as he also says: “You seek proof of Christ, who speaks to you through me.” And what does he say? “We shall be caught up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air.” And so half will be caught up, and half will be set before the fearsome judgment seat. As the Life-giver himself also says: “Truly I tell you, when the Son of Man comes, then, if two are in one bed, one will be taken and the other left. And if two are grinding at one mill, one will be lifted up and the other left.” And the apostles say to him: “Where, Lord?” And the Lord says: “Where the body is, there the eagles will gather.” Why eagles? Because they will be caught up into the heights.

What does it mean that two will be in one bed, and one will be taken and the other left, and that two will grind at one mill, and one will be lifted up and the other remain? There is no need here to explain one thing through another by an allegory; rather, the interpretation is plain. Scripture calls the ease of this world a bed, and the severe suffering of those who toil a mill: they remain bewildered, as though in a mill, amid various afflictions, passing from groaning to groaning and from poverty to poverty. And let Moses bear witness that Scripture calls severe suffering a mill. He says: “The angel went out and struck the firstborn of the Egyptians, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on the royal throne, to the firstborn of the captive who was at the mill.”

For this reason Isaiah also spoke reproachfully to the ruler of the Babylonians: “You said,” he says, “‘I am, and I shall remain forever’”—meaning, “I shall reign forever.” “For this reason childlessness will come upon you. Take a mill and grind flour.” For he said: “I shall hold my power and kingship forever, and I shall not see widowhood.” And he brings him down from the royal throne and binds him to the mill. “Take a mill,” he says, “grind flour; cross the river”—meaning, “You will wander about suffering and stumbling.”

And since beds signify rest and the mill signifies toil, the Life-giver makes clear that both among those who do not toil and among those who live at ease, some will be righteous and some sinful. Two will be in a bed: one, who is worthy of the faith, will be lifted up, and the other will belong to the demons. “And two,” he says, “will grind at one mill; one will be taken up and the other remain.” The disciples asked about this same meaning and said: “Lord, where will they be lifted up?” He says to them: “Where my body is”—meaning, “Where my coming will be.”

And he rightly said, “the body,” for he will be revealed in the body. Although the body was covered with divinity and suffused with the immortal root, [?] immortality itself, it did not lose its form. Rather, the form of the body remains, suffused and immersed in life. Let us bring forward an example of this. Although it may be obscure and faint, nevertheless, even in something small one can discern at least a few traces of something great. Take iron and plunge it into a fiery furnace, and see what it was like before it was plunged into the fire: dark in appearance and cold to the touch. After entering the fire, it is bright to look at and hot when examined. It has not ceased to be iron, but has received something beyond its own nature. Although it has become radiant, it has not departed from its own shape. Whatever shape you plunge into the furnace, that same shape appears: whether round, triangular, square, or whatever it may be, it does not change its shape. Only its color takes on the color of the fire. Likewise, the Lord’s holy body, worthy of worship, was suffused with the immortal root of godliness and immersed in life, and has clothed itself with divinity—not merely outwardly, but, like the iron, inwardly and outwardly. Yet its form remains uncorrupted, to the glory of those who believe and the shame of those who despise it.

And have you not seen how, when people return from a foreign land after a long time, their relatives seek a identifying sign—not some sign of their splendor, even if they return in splendor, but a sign of their former life, to determine whether this is truly the same person? They do not look so closely at their clothes as at the shape of their eyebrows, the distinguishing marks of their hands, and their hair—whether it is [?] or curly. Bodily defects become a herald identifying the unfamiliar person. For this reason, he does not wish to save the saints through divinity, but through the features of the body, so that they may look and see that he is indeed the one who was not believed before Caiaphas, was judged by Pilate, and went up on the cross. Thus his appearance will bear witness to the struggle against God, and his glory will reveal the truth. [?] God, how Peter will rejoice, and the apostles will dance and walk about, and say to one another: “This is our God! This is the one who was once crucified among us! This is the one who was once despised for our sake! Look at his features; pay attention to his eyes!”

And who had said this beforehand? Isaiah. “In the last days,” he says, “they will say, ‘Here is our God, in whom we hoped,’ and they will rejoice, and they will see eye to eye when the Lord has mercy on Zion.” This means that he will appear openly, directly before their eyes. The righteous rejoice and recognize their Lord; the wicked mourn when they recognize the one they despised. For if someone here in this world has wronged another, and then falls from honor and sees the person he wronged in authority, he becomes afraid and trembles, wondering whether that person will remember what happened and call the insult to mind. He devises all sorts of ways to calm his anger: can he persuade him personally, or through friends? But how will you persuade your Lord? Through the martyrs whom you slandered, or through the apostles whom you dishonored, whose names you defamed—the names of Matthew and Bartholomew—saying, ‘What do they have in common with Plato? How do they compare with Aristotle?’ Now you despise their names, and then you will run to seek shelter under their intercession—with what eyes, with what boldness? But do not think you can persuade him. Will you resort to flight? Will you not listen to David: ‘Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your presence?’ And if there is nowhere to flee, you poor, miserable person, learn to flee to him for refuge. Those who realize that they will not escape the punishments imposed by judges, as the laws rightly require, have only one refuge left: to appeal to the king and have the penalty of their torments removed by royal favor. Therefore David too, recognizing the remorse for his sins that tormented him, and that he deserved punishment according to the commands of the law, flees from everyone and takes refuge in the Lord alone, saying, ‘You, Lord, are my hope and my refuge.’

Jesus came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had turned the water into wine. Remember yesterday’s words: whatever is said in bodily terms must not be understood in bodily terms. Jesus came, not through a change in the power of his divinity, but through his body’s movement from place to place. For if his nature is unlimited in its divinity, then he is everywhere. He appears in the body sometimes here and sometimes there, carrying out the order of the divine plan, not changing in his nature. Jesus came and experienced weariness. He grew weary, not in his divine nature, but in his humanity. “Jesus came,” it says, “and was weary from the journey.” He grew weary in that which was capable of weariness, and not in his divinity, which never experiences weariness. The prophet also bears witness: “The eternal God,” he says, “who formed the ends of the earth, will neither hunger nor grow weary.” Yet here it says that he grew weary and hungered. “He fasted,” it says, “for forty days and forty nights, and afterward he hungered.” And it is clear that he hungered when he willed to do so. You see that the divine nature is free from needs, and that, according to the divine plan, he grows weary and hungers in the body.

And after saying, ‘Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven,’ what does he say? ‘Then all the nations of the earth will mourn.’ Severe mourning will come upon unbelievers, just as great joy will come upon believers. And it was not only the giver of life who said this, but before him the prophet Zechariah: ‘Then the sun will set over the prophets, and the moon will be darkened. Then they will see the one whom they pierced.’ This means the one whom they nailed to the cross with nails. ‘Then the families will mourn separately: the families of the house of David separately, and their wives separately; the families of the house of Nathan separately, and their wives separately; every family separately, and their wives separately.’ Why does he speak of all the families, or why does he mention David and Nathan? Nathan was not one of the patriarchs, but belonged to David’s family. David had two powerful sons. Although he had many sons, two were distinguished: Solomon and Nathan. Joseph’s family descends from Nathan, and Mary’s family is from Solomon. Mary was of royal descent, and although Joseph too was of royal descent, he was not descended from Solomon, who received David’s throne, but from Nathan, the king’s brother. And because the disgrace of fighting against God was to fall upon them all, and especially upon his relatives, who did not recognize their own Savior, he says, ‘The family of David will mourn separately.’ And because Christ was descended from David according to the flesh, his relatives mourn over what a guarantor of salvation they have lost.

And now, so that we may not mourn but rejoice together and receive the crucified one with glory, let the Jews who raised the body of the Son of God upon the cross hear this, and the heretics who despised his divinity. The writings of the prophets and the apostles will be opened before Christ’s tribunal. Do you suppose that the prophets will not come to the tribunal, that the Jews will not stand bowed before Christ’s judgment seat, and that the heretics will not be stricken and brokenhearted at the fearful judgment? The Jews will be questioned: “Why did you deny him?” The heretics will be questioned: “Why did you blaspheme?” And what answer will they be able to give? But perhaps the Jew will say, “I heard from the prophets: ‘I am God, and besides me there is no other God. I am the first, and I am the last.’ We learned this from the prophet Isaiah, and what could we wretched people have done?” And he will say to the heretics, “And why did you blaspheme the Son? Why did you insult the glory of the Only-begotten?” Perhaps they too will say, “Peter taught us this way, and Paul instructed us this way: Christ is our peace, who made the two one and reconciled us to the Father, as a mediator between God and human beings. He proclaimed him as a mediator, and not as God, and we were deceived.”

Then the companies of the prophets will become angry, and the ranks of the apostles will be enraged. They will bring out the books. Isaiah will open his book and say, “See, Lord, how I became a defender of your anointing. Let the declarations that I spoke about you be read. Let the Jews hear them; let the Christians say whether the apostles proclaimed anything more than I did. Did I not know you, the only-begotten Son of God? Did I not proclaim beforehand: ‘A child was born to us; a son was given to us. And his name is called Messenger of the Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Glorious, Prince of Peace, Father of the world to come’? Are not the proclamation of divinity and the saving dispensation distinct from one another? At one time: ‘God, Mighty, Glorious, Prince of Peace’; at another: ‘Behold, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,’ which translated means ‘God with us.’ Did I not also proclaim his sufferings: ‘He was led like a sheep to slaughter, and for the sins of the people he was handed over to death’? Did I not also proclaim his coming? Did I say, ‘A prophet is coming, and not God’? Just as the prophet Zechariah said, ‘Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes, riding on a donkey,’ so I too said, ‘Behold, the Lord comes with power.’ None of the apostles became a herald of you as I did. They proclaimed you together with your flesh and gave occasion for blasphemy through ignorance. But I proclaimed your divinity fully: ‘Messenger of the Great Counsel, God, Mighty, Glorious, Prince of Peace, Father of the world to come.’ None of your apostles said this. I became your herald before the apostles. Let no one slander my writings.” Isaiah says this with a fervent mind, for he is bold and impartial, just as the Apostle says, “Isaiah is bold and says.”

And Moses too comes forward, who was dearer and more honorable to the Jews than God. Stepping into their midst, he too becomes an advocate. He begins to say, “You miserable and wretched people!” For Moses’ [?] are different; he rebukes them gently. “The man Moses,” it says, “was gentler than all human beings.” “Did I not already foretell the barrenness of your unbelief? Because you could not accept greater things, I said, ‘The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you from your own people; listen to him. And every person who does not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed.’ And if you considered this a small thing, did I not proclaim the Trinity right at the beginning of the account of creation? Sometimes I said, ‘God said, Let there be light’; sometimes, ‘Let us make a human being according to the likeness of the image of our forms’; and sometimes, ‘Come, let us go down and divide their languages.’ Did I not write with my own hands that the Lord rained fire and sulfur from the Lord upon the people of Sodom and Gomorrah? Will I not grieve over your destruction? But I consider it better to disregard you and not stand against you [?].” And who will be a witness to this statement? The Lord himself, who said concerning the Jews, “Do you think that I will accuse you before the Father? There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you take pride. For if you believed Moses, you would also believe me, because he wrote about me.” And Daniel testifies that the books will be opened: “I watched as the Ancient of Days sat down, and his throne was like fire. I watched as thrones were cast down and books were opened.” They will say all these things concerning the Jews.

Let the heretics be called forward. Let Paul stand before them as their accuser, for he was slandered by their godless tongues. Let them also be called to account: “Where did you read that the Son is said to be inferior to the Father?” They say, “You and Peter taught this. He said, ‘Exalted at the right hand of God and having received the promise of the Spirit, he poured it out upon us.’ And again, ‘Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit.’ ‘God made that Jesus both Lord and Christ.’ And you said, ‘God the Father, who raised him from the dead.’ And again, ‘I thank God through Jesus Christ.’ And you did not say, ‘[?],’ but, ‘Through him I thank God.’” Then let Paul open his mouth, which was never closed, who said, “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians.” And let him rebuke them: “Son of lawlessness, wicked seed, plant of unbelief, did I not proclaim the divinity of the Only-begotten? Did I not say, ‘Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever’? Did I not say, ‘He did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant’? Did I not say, ‘There is neither barbarian nor savage nor Scythian, but Christ is all and in all’? Did I not say, ‘He is the radiance of glory, the imprint of his being, and the image of the invisible God, who upholds everything by his power’?” And they say, “Did you not proclaim him as a man? Did you not proclaim Christ according to the flesh?” “But although I proclaimed Christ according to the flesh, I also said elsewhere, ‘Even though we knew Christ according to the flesh, we no longer know him in that way.’” Let Peter also come forward and say, “You read about my accommodation to the Gentiles and the Jews, but did you not read the great confession I made concerning Christ? For which confession did I receive the keys? Was it because I called Jesus a Nazarene? No, but because I said, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ When I said, ‘He made him Lord and Christ,’ was it when the offspring was begotten of the Father?”

And now, be watchful, for the books and writings will be opened, and the King will sit, and the defenders of the truth will come forward, and the accusers will be put to shame. Let us act before the judgment. Before the King sits to judge, it is possible to win the Judge’s favor. Before the judgment, one can plead; before the fearsome judgment seat, there is no opportunity to make an appeal. May all of us appear blameless before the judgment seat of Christ, for his are glory and power forever. Amen.

And this is what is amazing: he grows weary so that he may give rest to the weary. “Come to me, you who are weary, and I will give you rest.” You see, then, that according to his divinity he gives rest to our weary nature, and according to his providential care he recognizes the needs of our humanity. Was he not able to move through the air the holy body which he took from us for our salvation, so that it would not suffer weariness? And did he not do something like this when he carried Habakkuk’s body from the land of Palestine to Babylon in a single instant? Through angelic grace he transported a man, a prophet, from one land to another; he suffered no weariness and felt no exertion. And could not the power of God himself grant his own body as much as the angel’s hand was able to accomplish? But there the necessities of the situation demanded speed, for in Babylon there was no worshiper of God to feed him. He saw that the prophet was in distress among the lions because he bore witness to the worship of God, and through an angel’s hand he seized the other prophet also and brought him there to that prophet. And see the wonder: it does not say that the angel carried him, but that he took him and set him there. See the angel’s power! Why are you astonished at the Creator of angels? He lifts and carries the prophet, not by supporting him beneath his feet and raising him upward, but by grasping his hair and snatching him away. And we know, brothers, how much pain the body suffers when someone is dragged by the hair. Yet the prophet crossed so many places and traveled so far, pulled by his hair, and suffered nothing; and in a single instant he took him and set him there. For it was an angel’s power, which not only lifted him but also granted lightness to his body. What was lifted was a body, but what lifted and carried it was a spirit. “He who made his angels spirits,” it says.

And do not be astonished that a light nature lifted a heavy body. First, even here among these created things that we can see, some things are heavy by nature, and some are light [?]. It does not depend on weight or size, but on the nature of created things, whatever they may be. Why is it that all the great trees—even if entire forests are cut down and fall into water—do not sink, while a great sea cannot keep one little needle, or a small [?] of iron, afloat? Thus it does not depend on size or weight, but on the Creator’s craftsmanship. Yet iron by itself has no means of remaining on the water, but with something light it stays on the water and is carried from place to place. They fill great ships with iron and take them wherever they wish; and because wood is light by nature, the light thing lifts the heavy thing. Take another example as well: a person cannot swim on the water for many hours, even if he knows the skill. Because he cannot keep exerting himself for long without resting, his arms grow weary, and he is forced to sink.

Just as a scorching wind first damages the root, and then the branches dry up along with it, so also in the worship of God: if the heart first becomes blind, then the fruit of the mouth dries up. However much the heretic’s tongue speaks slander, it becomes more and more unfruitful, as the prophet also says: “Ephraim’s head became diseased, and his root dried up, and he bears no fruit.” Yet one can often see outward forms of worship even among the enemies of the worship of God. There is a congregation in the church, and a congregation among the heretics; an altar here, and something called an altar there; true priests here, and false priests there. Here the gospel is believed, and there the gospel is mocked. Here the only-begotten Son of God is glorified, and there the only-begotten Son of God is treated as an enemy. Here the Holy Spirit rejoices in the flocks, and there the Holy Spirit is grieved by unbelief. For when the Holy Spirit sees ungodliness, he is grieved. For this reason Paul also says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, by whom you were sealed for the day of your redemption.”

Now, when you see among the heretics outward forms of religion resembling those of the church, do not be deceived by their appearance, but examine the truth. The Egyptian magicians also imitated the deeds of Moses, but these were appearances, not truth. Moses threw his staff onto the ground, and it became a serpent. The magicians also threw down their staffs, and they became serpents. Their appearances were alike, but the truth revealed the distinction between them, for Moses’ staff swallowed their staffs, showing that falsehood is swallowed up by truth. And so that you may know, brother, that every heretical opposition that draws up its battle line against the words of the apostles belongs to the same company as those magicians, listen to Paul: “Those who wish to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. But evil people and magicians will advance further into evil, being deceived and deceiving others. Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth: people whose minds are corrupted, unapproved in the faith.”

Pay close attention: he calls the opponents of the word of truth evil people and magicians. Why magicians? Because they deceive ignorant listeners, for the words of deceivers are sorcery to those who are deceived. For example, brothers, when people scratch their ears because they itch, scratching seems pleasant. But when they do it far too often, they cause sores, and the ears become deaf from the repeated scratching. Likewise, the words of heretics at first seem flattering to the ears, but afterward they deafen the senses. For this reason the apostle also says: “In the last times some will break away from the faith, following the itching of their ears.” What is this itching of the ears? Being deceived by fables. Everything the heretics say is fables. For this reason Paul also says: “They will turn their ears away from the truth and fall into fables.” Into which fables? Those of Arius, Macedonius, Montanus, the Manichaeans, and others like them, for they have all turned aside into fables and stand opposed to the truth. And he spoke not only of their opposition, but also of their breaking away. “But they will advance no further, for their foolishness will become apparent to everyone, as theirs also did.” We have the words of the apostles as pledges that put us on our guard. The physician of souls is a guarantor [?] with me, to dispel [?].

From now on, do not let the outward appearances of heretics who revile godliness deceive you. For among the Jews too, many had the outward forms of godliness, but there was no zeal for truth in them. Isaiah compares them to an unwatered garden and to a leafy tree in which there is no fruit. He says, “They shall be like a terebinth stripped of its leaves, and like an unwatered garden.” The community of heretics is also an unwatered garden. It is not watered by the water of life, of which the Giver of Life says, “Whoever believes in me, as the Scriptures say, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” Jesus said this about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed were to receive.

See how they are an unwatered garden. He did not say, “Like a garden that does not know water,” but, “Like an unwatered garden.” They say that the Holy Spirit exists, but they do not have him. They preach, but they do not enjoy the gifts of the Spirit, for the Holy Spirit does not dwell in ungrateful souls. As long as godliness is in a person, the Holy Spirit dwells there; and when godliness departs, the Holy Spirit also departs. Indeed, we must conclude that all human souls receive either the Holy Spirit after grace or an unclean spirit. I do not mean that the Holy Spirit performs prophetic or apostolic works in a person. Rather, if someone does not have faith—for faith is a gift of the Spirit—he does not have the Holy Spirit. Even if someone is an insignificant layperson, indeed among the very least, and has only faith in Christ, the Holy Spirit is in him. No one can call Jesus Lord except by the Holy Spirit. The soul must either be enlightened by the Holy Spirit or come under the power of unclean spirits. And who is there who would say this? When King Saul acted lawlessly and presumed to turn his mind to the unapproachable mystery, which it was not lawful for him to offer, he who had once slaughtered mediums and diviners then himself sought refuge with diviners. And what do the Scriptures say? “The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an unclean spirit tormented him.”

THE HEAVENS REJOICE when stars rise among stars, and harbors when small ships gleam among great ships, and when clouds play up and down among clouds and scatter showers of sweet dew. The church also rejoices when congregations hasten after congregations and feasts press upon feasts in the holy places. They do not change their powers according to the places, but renew their affection as the places change: from blessing to blessing, from church to church. Rather, we ought to say, in the Apostle’s words, from faith to faith and from glory to glory. And the prophetic saying is fulfilled: “They shall go from strength to strength.” Yesterday the royal crown of the apostles made us radiant, and today the crown of the martyrs enlightens us. The church receives both the royal crown and the victor’s crown, and in it the prophet’s saying is fulfilled: “The church is a crown of beauty in the Lord’s hand, and a royal diadem in the hand of God.” May our bosoms be crowned with the labors of these martyrs, and the walls of this temple with the lights of lamps, both a rampart and a bulwark. A double bulwark from the Trinity has been placed around us, for nothing in heaven or on earth can be enlightened without the Holy Trinity. These new things imitate the original pattern, for what God does invisibly, these lamps do visibly: this illumination has surrounded us like a bulwark. For he promises, “I will be a wall of fire around my people.”

The brothers hated Joseph because of his dreams, and they did not know that they were hating not him but the one who showed him the dreams. Surely he did not see the dream by his own will! Therefore, whoever fought against the dreamer was fighting against God. But see how wickedness blinds people! Why do you fight against this dreamer? Will the outcomes of these dreams prove true or false? If they prove true, by what devices can you set aside the truth? And if they prove false, why should you envy this person who babbles about his nighttime fancies? Joseph went to visit his brothers, to show an act of love, and they repaid his kindness with the insult of ingratitude. He spoke words of peace to them, but they gathered for conflict and fought against him, so that the saying of the giver of life might be fulfilled: “They hated me without cause.” See the wonders: “The dreamer is coming,” they say. The dream’s vision terrified them—or rather, not the vision, but the fear that these things would come to pass. They plotted the holy man’s death, and God made their wickedness into an instrument of providence. For it is God’s work not only to bestow gifts of his own, but also to turn our wickedness to good use. They wanted to kill their brother. Reuben offered good counsel: “Let us not kill him, for he is our brother and our flesh. Instead, let us throw him into one of the pits somewhere.” He had it in mind to find a way to save him, but in fact he was carrying out the work of providence. Joseph was not killed, but went down alive into the pit, for he was a foreshadowing of the living one who descended alive into Hades. Joseph went down into the pit, and the pit was empty of water: a likeness of the tomb of the giver of life, which was empty of the dead.

Joseph was thrown into the pit. Judah, moved with pity for his brother, put forward a good proposal: not to kill him in the pit. “What profit would there be if we killed him? Come, let us sell him.” Judah spared his brother out of concern, but the all-knowing God was carrying out the work of providence. Joseph had to be sold at that time through Judah, because the Life-giver too was sold through Judas the betrayer. The Ishmaelites took him and brought him to Egypt. By what means? By camel. And what were the camels carrying? Resin, [?], and incense. Indeed, it was fitting to send [?] oil in its humiliation along with incense. We can understand from the account itself how wickedness unwillingly praises the one being sold, so that they may receive a higher price. The Ishmaelites asked, “Is this young man good?” They were compelled to comply, for they saw the silver in their hands. “He is freeborn,” they said, “and noble. He does not know how to steal; he cannot swear falsely.” Willingly, against its will, wickedness exposed its own falsehood.

Joseph went down to Egypt, because the Life-giver too was to go to Egypt. Joseph was sold to foreigners; Christ was handed over to the Gentiles: “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of the Gentiles.” Joseph was in the hands of the Ishmaelites, and Jesus in the hands of the Gentiles. Joseph went down to Egypt and was afflicted at first, for Jesus too was not accepted by the Gentiles at first, and afterward they worshiped the one whom they had persecuted and insulted. The image was accurately depicted in Joseph’s suffering from the lust of winter [?]. The woman seized Joseph’s clothes, just as death seized the Life-giver’s body. Joseph stripped off his clothes and left them with the wanton woman, just as the Life-giver, when he rose, left his clothes in the tomb. Joseph entered prison, because Christ too was to enter the tomb. Joseph was ruler over the prisoners, because Christ too is king of the living and the dead.

And see the nobility of his spirit. Outwardly he was in prison and in chains; the free man was in slavery, and the man destined to be honored with kingship was in prison. He never doubted like someone weak in faith. He did not say, “What of the dreams [?]? Where are the false visions? Where are God’s foretelling declarations? You promised me kingship, yet I am compelled to serve. You promised to give me authority as a gift, yet I do not even enjoy the freedom common to everyone. I descended from freedom into slavery; I went from ease into prison.” He entertained no such thought, but persevered and awaited the fulfillment of events. And who will testify that he looked forward to the fulfillment of events and did not doubt? There were, it says, two servants of Pharaoh in the prison. They had dreams and were sad. Joseph said to them, “Why are you sad?” And they said, “We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them.” He did not say, “Let no one pay attention to dreams. Let my dreams serve as an example of other dreams.” Instead, to make it clear that he was intent on the fulfillment of his own dreams, he said, “Tell me, and I will explain them to you.” Have your own dreams come to pass at all, that you should interpret those of others? He interprets their dreams and looks forward to the fulfillment of his own.

Pay close attention; turn from the figure to the reality. If you wish to learn about Joseph’s character, do not learn it from his brothers, for envy conceals the truth and casts the free man into slavery. Nor from the Ishmaelites, for they too bought the free man as a slave. Nor from his mistress, for she slandered him because of her own shamelessness. But if you wish to understand what sort of person Joseph was, ask his father, and he says, “He is a son, and a beloved son.”

Come to Christ. If you wish to understand what sort of person Christ is, do not learn it from the Jews, for envy disguises the truth. Nor from the idolaters, for they hate the destroyer of their images. Nor from the schismatics, because just as the Ishmaelites did not know that they had bought a free man, so the schismatics do not recognize him, and therefore make the free man a slave. Nor from the Jews, for they are enemies of the cross. Nor from the idolaters, for they hate the one who exposes their idols. Nor from the heretics, for they are like Ishmael, who was not born of the free woman but of the slave woman. The Ishmaelites are a figure of the schismatics, and the children of the free woman are a figure of believers.

When the patriarch blessed Joseph, he said, “Your blessing is from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth.” Pay attention: these are God’s gifts, bestowed from heaven and earth. The gifts were not given to Ishmael, for he did not possess them. “By the sword,” he says, “you shall live.” The Ishmaelites have no other occupation by which they can make any profit, except the sword alone. Like them are the schismatics, who believe neither the declarations from heaven nor the prophets, but bring the sword against them. And fittingly so, for they are Ishmaelites: they live not by the word of God, but by the sword of folly.

From now on, do not learn what Christ is like from Jews, idolaters, or heretics. Instead, if you wish to understand, learn his characteristics from his own root. See what his Father testifies about him: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” The Father calls him Son, and do you call him a creature? “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son.” And again: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.” Does the Father not convince you? Do the declarations of the prophets not make you stand in awe? Do the ranks of the apostles not inspire reverence in you? Let the demons put you to shame. For you heed neither the Father, who says, “This is my beloved Son,” nor Paul, who proclaims, “You are the Son of the living God,” nor Isaiah, who calls him mighty God. You have denied the Scriptures; at least show some reverence before the demons. Matthew says: “Demons came out of many people and cried out, ‘You are the Son of God.’” Likewise, Mark says that they agreed in their words and said: “We know who you are, the Son of God.” Likewise, Luke declares that when the demons saw him, they fell down before him, cried out, and said: “We know who you are, the Son of God. [?] before the time to judge us.” The demons confess him as the Son of God, and do you call him a creature? You are in great distress, for you make the demons appear more righteous than yourself: an abundance of evil makes those with less evil appear righteous. For this reason, because of Jerusalem’s abundance of evil, he said to her: “Sodom has been shown to be more righteous than you.” This was another way of saying: “Compared with your sins, the city of the Sodomites appeared righteous.”

You have the example; bow down before the truth. For if Joseph had not gone to Egypt, the land of the Egyptians would have died of hunger. And if the giver of life had not come into the world, the whole world would have died from hunger for the divine word. And to learn that God, the divine Word, is food, listen: “Behold, I will send you not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord.” Oh, what wonders! How the example was depicted beforehand in the prophet! You have seen the example in Joseph; see also the example of the resurrection in Daniel. They cast Daniel into the pit, against the will of Darius and Cyrus. Christ went up onto the cross with Pilate’s reluctant consent. The united body of officials compelled King Darius, and the united body of Jews compelled Pilate. Darius went early to see the pit and Daniel, to find out whether he was safe. The apostles and the women went early to the tomb to see whether the living one was alive.

Turn, heretics, from unbelief to faith. Do not be worse than water. Water saw Jesus and became wine; yet you say “Son” and call him a servant. He performed his first sign in Cana of Galilee, so that the saying might be fulfilled: “Galilee of the Gentiles—the people who sat in darkness saw a great light.” The first sign took place at a wedding, because the human race first increases through marriage, and a wedding is the root of the human plant. He blesses the root so that he may bless its shoots. And I marvel at this: not merely that he was invited and agreed to go, but that he went not to some distinguished house where a wedding was taking place, but to a wedding in the house of a poor man. The man in whose house the wedding took place was poor—so poor that even the little wine ran out. He was poor in possessions, but became rich in the treasures of truth.

The Lord appeared and changed the water into wine. His mother reminded him: “They have no wine,” she said. She was his mother according to the flesh and his servant according to his divinity. She was his servant according to his divine nature and became his mother according to the arrangement of his incarnation. He was both her God and her son: her God according to his lordship, and her son according to the arrangement of his incarnation. “They have no wine.” “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” At this point some understood him to be promising something different. But he was reproaching his mother, because she still regarded the Lord of mankind as a mere man. He rebuked her, not because she reminded him, but because she reminded him as though he were a man. Many thought that “My hour has not yet come” meant, “The time for miracles has not yet come.” But if it had not come, how could you perform the miracle? Rather, he was reproaching his mother for reminding him needlessly and at an unsuitable time, and because God has no need to be reminded. “The time for my revelation has not yet come, for no one yet knows who I am.” And so that you may learn that he said those words not to [?] the miracle, but because she had called attention to his power, his mother, understanding his dignity, said: “Do whatever he tells you.”

He spoke and changed the water into wine—he who turns water into oil. For through the olive tree he turns dew into oil, and through [?] into wheat, and through other plants into aromatic herbs, and through trees into fruit; and in all things he gives every plant its own flavor. There is one rain, but many different flavors are produced. Do not marvel only because he changed water into wine. Rather, marvel greatly because throughout creation he turns the same rain into different colors and flavors, and blood into milk, and all these things, too, into their own colors and flavors. Through daily familiarity people treated his great works with contempt, while something new in an unexpected act of his providence seemed marvelous. Otherwise, why do you not marvel at how he turns blood in women’s breasts into the white substance of milk? Why are you not astonished that he changes dark hair into white, something that the skill of dyers is wholly unable to accomplish? It is possible to dye something white black, but to make something black white is utterly impossible. Blood cannot be dyed, nor can something once dyed red be turned white. Yet he turns dark blood into white blood and changes black hair into white hair, so that you may learn that nature does not bring this about by itself; rather, he established the rule that nature should be this way.

So when you see him going to a wedding and making water into wine, marvel. But know that these are only tastes of his great works. It is great, though not in comparison with the wonder-worker; rather, we enjoy it because of his love. It is therefore right and fitting to understand that the miracles of the giver of life were very small in relation to him, but very great for those who benefited from them. Moses bears witness that this is so when he recounts to them the miracles performed in the land of the Egyptians: “Remember how the Lord your God brought you out of the land of the Egyptians with great signs and awesome deeds.” See how he marveled at the miracles. See also how the worker of miracles considers the deeds small: “I did all these things to the Egyptians so that you might tell your children’s children how I played with the Egyptians.” Do you see? What seems miraculous to us is play to God. But enough of this for now.

Truly, the earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, like abundant waters covering the seas. Even now, through the holy congregations, the prophet’s hidden saying is fulfilled: “The earth is the Lord’s, with all its fullness.” The prophets proclaimed this, but they did not speak these words with reference to the present established state of things. Who does not know that the earth is the Lord’s, with all its fullness? Or who doubts whether another lord has a share in creation? For all of us, believers and unbelievers alike, plainly know through long-established habit that everything belongs to God. But the prophets did not say this with reference to the present established state of things, but with reference to the former error, when idolatry [?] the earth, when people burned with zeal for images, when God was not recognized and those who were not gods received worship.

May the light of Christ dawn upon us, and may the divine word illuminate our souls, so that we may strip off the works of darkness and put on the works of light, make our preaching shine through our words, and adorn with our deeds the promise we have made; so that through words, deeds, and faith, and with God's approval, we may send up glory to the all-holy Trinity forever. Amen.

When, as the Apostle says, “They worshiped the creation and not the Creator,” the holy prophets saw the earth as though driven into exile by some tyrant. They cried out to those who had gone astray: “The earth is the Lord’s, with all its fullness. Why do you wander in error? Why do you reckon the regions of the earth to belong to various gods?” For the places were named after the demons. Just as a rebel invades by force and drives out another’s kingdom for his own sake, so the demons entered the world and seized its various regions for themselves. Some were called gods of the Lycians, some of the people of Attica, others of the [?], and others of the Achaeans. Each was allotted its own region, and the places were named after the designation of the gods to whom they were dedicated. For example, the Athenians were named after the god whom they worshiped, and Heliopolis after its own god, and each people after its own gods. To avoid lengthening this account by listing them, the places too were named after the gods.

And so that the earlier account may not mislead you in any way, pay attention to the writings that agree with it. The ancients thought that each of the gods had received one region of the earth, and that God possessed the region of Judea. For the Assyrian himself said, when they came against the land of the Palestinians, “Did their gods save their respective countries, that the God of Israel should save you?” The ancients thought that the Lord of all was one of those supposed gods. And just as each of those falsely called gods received his own country, so God possessed the country of the Palestinians as his own particular domain. As the other barbarian also said, he had authority only over the mountains of the Palestinians.

Now, to those misguided people who divided the earth from its one sovereign and reckoned the regions under heaven to be under many dominions, they cried out, “The earth, with all its fullness, belongs to the Lord.” Then, as though required to make clear why the whole earth belongs to the Lord, he brings forward the familiar facts of creation to establish the extent of his dominion. “He himself,” he says, “laid its foundations upon the sea and established it upon the rivers.”

From then on, the whole earth was filled with the glory of Christ, and the whole earth became full of the knowledge of the Lord. As the prophet Isaiah says, “Like the many waters that cover the seas.” The laws of faith establish a rule that nature does not admit. You know, brothers, that many rivers from every region under heaven flow into the seas, yet they have not covered them. Rather, they themselves have been covered, and have not covered the seas. But the new proclamation promises a new kind of power. “The knowledge of God,” he says, “filled the earth like the many waters that cover the seas.” What cannot happen by nature, he establishes through knowledge. Just as the sea cannot be covered by waters from elsewhere, so, according to the ordinary course of things, the earth cannot be filled with knowledge. But look: the word has spread and filled all the ends of the earth, and the teaching of the gospel has covered the seas.

Which sea? The one in which people were tossed about as in an abyss. The word of God went forth and filled every region under heaven. And what Daniel said was fulfilled: “The stone that was cut from the mountain without hands became a great mountain, and the whole earth was filled by it.” At times he compares it to waters that cover everything under heaven, for the teaching advanced on its course, and the word fills the ends of the earth; and at times to a mountain, because of the height of the teaching, because its speech about God reaches heaven. “In the last days,” he says, “the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, and the house of God above the summits of the mountains.”

Which house? The church. For it is not built upon mountains, but stands established in the height of its speech about God. The church is the house of God, as Paul writes to Timothy: “So that you may know,” he says, “how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the church.” And why is it upon the mountains? The Savior says, “A city standing upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

There was a stone that was cut out without hands, for Christ was born without a man. The stone was cut out without hands, for Christ was born without marital union. And the stone became a great mountain and filled everything beneath heaven. But lest anyone consider these words forced and say, “What connection does a stone have with establishing a birth in the flesh?” we must also make it clear that human offspring are called stones hewn from rock. From this it will be established that being cut out means being born. The prophet Isaiah says to the people, “Look to the solid rock from which you were hewn.” And to explain the rock, he adds, “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah, who gave birth to you.” Do you see that he calls human offspring stones hewn from rock?

And why does he speak of the people's offspring as coming from a rock? Because Sarah was barren. A rock too is barren and bears no fruit. He calls her a rock because she was barren by nature but able to bear children by grace. “Look,” he says, “to the rock from which you were hewn.” Just as the stones hewn from rock there signify the people's offspring, so here the stone cut out without hands signifies Christ's birth in the flesh. And see how carefully he speaks. For rocks often break off and fall from mountains without hands, but he did not say that it broke off or split apart, but that it was cut out. Since he was to speak of the birth ordained by divine providence, he says, “The stone was cut out without hands.” For he was not born according to the laws of nature, but through a new kind of travail [?], and without experience of marital union the flower blossomed from a virgin womb. And it became a great mountain and filled the earth. If the events did not agree with the words, then this defense is in vain, and we are trying to force the truth by falsehood. But if the events shine forth and cry aloud before the words, and the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of Christ, then, if we are ungrateful for the benefits of these accomplishments, we too shall hear from the Lord, “Even if you are silent, these stones will cry out.” A stone was cut out without hands and became a great mountain. And all peoples hasten to this mountain and say, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.”

And pay close attention to how he first announces the conversion of the Gentiles and then the calling of the Jews. For first some of the Gentiles believe in Christ, and after them some of the Jews. “Many nations will follow and say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and he will tell us his ways, and we will walk with him.’” And what does he add after this? “For the law,” he says, “will go forth from Zion.” See how he announces the law of the second covenant, for the first law came not from Zion but from Mount Sinai. “The law,” he says, “will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he will judge among the nations”—and the other things that follow, one by one. When he has foretold the conversion of the Gentiles, the prophetic Spirit then calls out to the Jews and says, “And now, house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord.” Do you see? First the Gentiles believe, and then the Jewish people are called.

You have the example of Joseph. The foreshadowings of the giver of life were fulfilled beforehand: Joseph first ruled in Egypt, and then over his ungrateful brothers; he first ruled over the Egyptians, who were foreigners, and then over his brothers, who were of his own people. And see the wonders: will not everything that David said be fulfilled completely in Christ? “He established it,” he says, “as a testimony in Joseph.” This is another way of saying that he placed in Joseph a prophecy that would bear witness. If Joseph had stayed with his father Jacob, Egypt would not have received the one who would provide for it. Pay close attention: if Joseph had remained there, cherished by his father, Egypt would not have received its guardian, the one who devised a remedy for the famine. Joseph was sent to visit his brothers and the flocks; the Only-begotten was sent into the world to seek the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Dreams adorned Joseph, and miracles glorified Christ. “I saw that my brothers and I were reaping, and their sheaves bowed down to my sheaf.” Since they would bow down because of the danger of famine, God showed beforehand, through the sheaves of grain, the outcome of the events to come. First the sheaves bowed down to him, because first his brothers would bow down to him. The circumstances of the famine first brought them down to Egypt, and on the second occasion they recognized their brother. The first time they stood trembling before him as before a ruler; on the second occasion they recognized him and were honored. They recognized him and were glorified as the brothers of the glorified Joseph.

The enemy of truth saw the Lord and Savior, the life-giving God, being proclaimed, and was troubled. He saw the Lord’s coming on a donkey, glorified by us as before, and tried to cause turmoil with the clatter of rattling chariots, to hinder the advance of the donkey. Yet the donkey, walking gently and with a peaceful tread, checked the chariot steeds of the warriors. For he knew that the donkey had been prepared to defeat the chariots and steeds. For the Savior came on a donkey not to show any weakness, but the gentleness of humility, so that he might extinguish arrogance. And because the enemy knew that these things would happen according to the prophetic utterance, he became jealous and raged against the donkey. Yet this was to extinguish the pride of the proud one and bring low the immense arrogance of the one who exalted himself in chariots and steeds.

The blessed prophet rightly announced this beforehand and gave encouragement, saying: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; proclaim and rejoice, daughter of Jerusalem. For behold, your king comes, riding on the foal of a donkey, to destroy the chariots from Ephraim and the steeds from Jerusalem.” Do you see how he softened and brought down swaggering arrogance through gentleness? Just as he removed sufferings through suffering, bound death through death, and exposed the power of the adversary through the wood of the holy cross, so also through the donkey he broke the horse-borne insolence of the one who boasted.

“Rejoice,” says the prophet, “daughter of Zion; exult and proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem.” For it is right and fitting for those who worship God not only to possess the divine gifts themselves, but also to spread the proclamation of his goodness to others. “For behold, your king comes, gentle and humble, seated on a donkey.” He rightly placed “gentle” and “humble” first, to make clear that these were not signs of poverty, but tidings of gentleness and humility. For if someone rides a young donkey because he lacks possessions and has no steeds, this is not counted as goodness and humility, since the constraint of destitution brings him to it. But if someone who has chariots and many steeds sits on a donkey’s foal out of gentleness, he adorns the practice of gentleness with humility. The King of hosts did not lack chariots. The Only-Begotten did not lack chariots and steeds; of him the prophet says, “The chariots of God are ten thousandfold, and thousands are their drivers.” He did not lack chariots, he who harnesses the winds and speeds along with wondrous and unprecedented bridles. Or do you not know that, just as horses serve as mounts for us, [?], according to what David says: “He who rides upon the wings of the winds”?

Now he came on a donkey to overthrow pride through humility and also to proclaim fully, in a figure, the entry of the Gentiles. For the donkey is counted among the unclean animals: Moses set apart as unclean every animal that neither has a divided hoof nor chews the cud. And the donkey, because it neither chews the cud nor has a divided hoof, is counted among the unclean animals. He was fulfilling beforehand the figures of his dispensation that seeks out humanity, for he was going to call the divine, holy people his mount. Just as horses are mounts for a rider, so the souls of the saints are mounts for riders; so also the souls of the saints are mounts for God in their conduct and obedience to his instructive commands. As the prophet says, “You will mount your horses, and your riding brings salvation.” Paul was such an unbroken, unbridled mount, heedless of the divine laws. He grazed in the pastures of the law and kicked against the graces of the gospel. When the Son, the Lord of all, put a bridle on him and mounted him, he said, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad and to kick against the sword.” And since the donkey has bolted and run away from the course of this discourse, let us beseech the Lord of the donkey, who can hold it, lead it, and keep the donkey within the discourse. For he is the one of whom the prophecy says, “He will tie his donkey to the vine.”

Jesus sat on a donkey—he who sits upon the cherubim, who above is awesome because of his divine nature and below is longed for because of his grace and love for humanity. On high the seraphim bow before him with trembling, and on earth he is boldly proclaimed by us who are flesh. For just as his birth above is awesome, so below the freely springing shoot is an object of longing. Jesus sat on a donkey, and the crowds spread their garments before him. The honor was [?], but the honor offered by those honoring him was in no way worthy according to the commandment. For God does not seek gifts from human beings according to his own worthiness, but according to the means of those honoring him. Indeed, there is nothing that could honor God according to his own worthiness. Neither the whole earth nor all heaven joining their voices, nor all the voices of angels and archangels, nor visible and invisible beings becoming tongues, are sufficient to glorify him according to his own worthiness.

He rode on a donkey, he who sits eternally in the heavens. People spread their garments before him, though they ought to have spread out their souls before their garments. You who spread your garments for the donkey to tread upon, spread out your soul as a dwelling for God. This is what John the Baptist also proclaimed: “Prepare the ways of the Lord, and make the [?] paths straight.” This means making souls ready, so that God and the Son of the Lord may enter and dwell in them. Taking palm branches, they went out to meet him. And the one whom the angels glorify in heaven with awe, the children also blessed, rejoicing on earth and saying, “Hosanna!” In the Hebrew language this signifies glorification and great praise.

Then the emperor, filled with anger, sent for the patriarch of the city and assailed him harshly with severe insults, saying, “You have turned the bishops away—the very bishops who, after much hard work, had barely agreed [?] to join us. Now you have turned them away from us!” In his agitation, he ordered the senate to enter the episcopal residence and judge the events that had taken place between them. The patriarch himself was also to stand trial, and if they found him at fault, he too was to be condemned.

At that time Conon was also arrested. He was the leader of the heresy of those who dare to count natures, substances, godheads, and gods in the holy Trinity, which is equal in substance. He too was arrested and imprisoned for a time in the episcopal residence, along with the others. They demanded that he draw up a written declaration as a heretic, but he resisted this and did not do it. When the victorious emperor learned of this, he swore by the Mother of God, saying, “Even if he appeals and enters the church and receives communion without drawing up a declaration of repentance, I will not enter it or receive communion in it.” Thus, because he was a heretic and a blasphemer, when Photius, the son of Belisarius’s wife, came to the imperial city at that time, Conon was handed over to him. He took him with him to Palestine and imprisoned him in the monastery called the New Monastery. He remained there for three years. Then he was released and went to the region of Cilicia.

Chapter Nine. “Why do you sit as a Christian with those who sent me to you, yet judge God’s servants like a pagan? You are not among living human beings unless you quickly burn me, a feeble old man, and eat me roasted.” When the prefect heard this, he was moved by respect for his old age. He ordered him to be taken out of his presence and brought to the bishop. The bishop, in the madness [?] of his anger, sent him away and imprisoned him in Heraclea, a city in Thrace. He remained there for two years, without being allowed to see any of his acquaintances. Since he was given no change of clothing and was infested with countless lice, one of his disciples went out and brought him a change. After that, no further change was allowed to be given to him, even through someone else. Later he became mortally ill. He forbade, under pain of anathema, his burial by adherents of the synod, or any of them ministering or offering prayer over him. So the orthodox [?] officers of the Roman army who were there took him out and buried him with candles and abundant perfumes. They wrapped and honored his body as that of a great martyr. They complained and spoke bitterly against the persecution of people such as these. Some of the faithful in the city planned to go out and take the holy man’s body.
13. Chapter Thirteen: About Sergius and Sergius, our priests, and the beatings and imprisonments they endured.
17. Chapter Seventeen: About how, as a result of this, persecutions were stirred up everywhere.

As a result of this persecution, which had been stirred up in the imperial city and was being carried out so zealously, tyrannically, and unceasingly, a fierce persecution was now stirred up throughout all the territories of the Romans, wherever orthodox believers were found. Persecution was stirred up against them through letters from John the patriarch and the others. It rose like the waves of the sea, and like the Babylonian furnace with its great blaze. But unlike that furnace, it was not fueled with reeds, branches, and other materials. This one was fueled with anger, fury, and zeal for destruction and killing, and it blazed terribly and fiercely. With these came all their accompanying evils: the plundering of movable belongings and the seizure of property on this pretext; and, secondly, confinement in cramped prisons and harsh bonds, tortures, beatings, banishments, and the rest, in every region and city and their districts.

Then all the Magi gathered and said to Khosrow their king, “O king, live forever! We have learned that the emperor of the Romans demands, compels, and forces everyone throughout his dominion to adopt his religion and his faith. He demands that the many people throughout all his territories worship—worship according to his religion. Everyone who refuses to obey him he expels and drives out of his entire dominion. Let your own divinity likewise command that the same be done in your dominion: that all religions turn to your religion, and that everyone in your dominion practice your worship. Those who dare to oppose your command must not live.”

When King Khosrow heard these things from the Magi, he yielded to their words and accepted their advice. Immediately he too began with the Christians. First he sent and seized three bishops, along with many clergy and a large crowd of people [?]. He commanded them to renounce their faith and join him in worshiping fire, the sun, and the other objects of his worship. But they disputed with him and courageously stood against him, declaring, “We are Christians, O king [?]. We worship and honor God, the maker of heaven, earth, the seas, and everything in them. We will not abandon him, the creator of everything, and worship his creatures. Do not be mistaken, O king. You have authority over our bodies, to do whatever you wish to them. But our souls belong to him and are in his hands, and you have absolutely no authority over them.”

When the king heard these things, along with many other words befitting the bishops’ witness, he gave orders, and immediately they were flayed and died. He also committed many other evil acts against the Christians, and destroyed many monasteries and churches. He bound and imprisoned many people, and his heart became arrogant.
